source: Schaafstal, Schraagen and van Berlo (2000) Cognitive task analysis and innovation of training (Human Factors 42(1) 75-86); re-check of University of Twente Pure page, TNO repository and Crossref record
finding: Second attempt to find the numbers failed. Every accessible record (Pure, TNO, Crossref) carries only the abstract. The full text is behind a paywall and the TNO PDF link returns a web page, not a PDF.
numbers: Abstract only: two observational studies plus literature review; trained group solved 'twice as many malfunctions' in less time; less training time. No N, no error counts, no effect size, no test statistics visible anywhere I could open. Crossref lists 25 references.
quote: technicians trained in structured troubleshooting solve twice as many malfunctions, in less time
limits: Gap 4 stays open. I did not find any replication of the structured troubleshooting evaluation; the citation lists (OpenAlex) were not reachable because the free API budget was used up.
agent_relevance: Do not cite a number for the founding human result beyond 'about 2x'. Treat the method-plus-system-breakdown advantage as unquantified in our notes.

source: Jonassen and Hung (2006) Learning to troubleshoot: a new theory-based design architecture, Educational Psychology Review 18(1) 77-114
finding: Opened the publisher page: abstract, figure list and paywall notice. The paper is a design proposal, not an experiment. It names three parts: a multi-layered conceptual model of the system (topographic, function, strategic, procedural views), a simulator where the learner must generate, reconcile, test and interpret hypotheses, and a case library with a case-based reasoning engine that tells stories of past troubleshooting as advice.
numbers: No participants, no scores, no effect sizes in the abstract. Springer shows 4 figures and 93 citations; OpenAlex lists the article as closed access with 126 citations. A secondary blog summary (opened, a17) also reports no empirical test.
quote: query experienced troubleshooters about what they would do
limits: Full text paywalled; I could not read the body or the reference list. I cannot rule out that the body reviews earlier empirical studies. What I can say: the architecture itself is presented as untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 is mostly closed: the case-library design is a theory proposal with no evaluation in the accessible text. Our scaffold should treat 'ask what an expert would do' as a hypothesis to test, not a proven operator.

source: Van Gog, Paas and Van Merrienboer (2005) Uncovering expertise-related differences in troubleshooting performance: combining eye movement and concurrent verbal protocol data, Applied Cognitive Psychology 19, 205-221
finding: Abstract (via Crossref) says higher-expertise people spent relatively more time in the problem-orientation phase, had shorter mean fixation duration there, and fixated more on a major fault-related component. In problem formulation their fixations were longer. In action evaluation they again spent relatively more time. Only mean fixation duration differed significantly over the phases.
numbers: No N, means or test values in the abstract. The abstract calls the expertise differences 'relatively small'.
quote: higher expertise participants spent relatively more time
limits: Abstract only; the Wiley PDF returned HTTP 403. Gap 9 only partly closed: direction known, size not. Domain is electrical circuit troubleshooting, small expertise gap.
agent_relevance: Supports giving S1 (orientation) real time and a fixation on the fault-related part before hypothesising. The effect is small, so do not over-weight it.

source: FaulT-Bench (2026) Towards benchmarking network troubleshooting LLM agents under unreliable user tickets, arXiv 2608.27021
finding: 200 emulated-network scenarios, 3 agents (SADE, Claude Code baseline, ReAct), 3 passes. With a real fault and an accurate ticket the task is nearly solved. With a healthy network and a false ticket, agents disprove the symptom but keep probing until they can blame a benign condition. The authors say the agents lack a criterion for concluding that no fault exists.
numbers: Outcome on 80 Correct-Fault: SADE 0.912, CC-Baseline 0.942, ReAct 0.941 (mean 0.932). 72 False-Premise: mean 0.820 (SADE 0.745, CC-B 0.870, ReAct 0.848). Over-diagnosis on healthy networks, standard ticket: SADE 24% (51/210 answered runs), ReAct 16% (33/209), CC-B 11% (21/198). Wrong-Device 24 scenarios mean 0.957; Wrong-Cause 24 mean 0.911. Timeouts 2-5% on standard tickets. 3,960 runs, US$1,525.
quote: What the agents lack is a criterion for concluding, with evidence, that no fault exists.
limits: Benchmark measures the failure; it does not test a fix (no 'no fault' exit or verify gate arm). The structured agent (SADE) over-diagnoses most, so structure alone does not cure it. Scoring uses one LLM judge (gpt-5-mini) with fixed prompts; I found no human agreement check. Same research group as SADE (first author Tseng, senior author Seneviratne on both arXiv records), so SADE's weakness here is self-reported, which makes it more credible, but this is not an independent replication of SADE's gains. Authors say 8% of (scenario, agent) cells move by 0.5 or more between passes.
agent_relevance: Strong case for an explicit healthy-system exit in S4 with a stated stopping criterion. Gap 2 stays open as an intervention test, but the problem is now measured: 11-24% false alarms on clean systems.

source: FaulT-Bench (2026) persona rewrites and cost analysis (E2, Tables 5, 6, 8)
finding: Over-diagnosis depends on how checkable the ticket is, not on how confident the reporter sounds. Vague tickets with no identifiers push false alarms up and cost more. Confidence in the wrong ticket helped agents because they could refute a definite claim.
numbers: Same 72 healthy networks. Mean outcome / over-diagnosis (all agents): Standard 0.820 / 17%; Naive 0.820 / 16%; Novice 0.675 / 31%; Novice-confident 0.714 / 28%; Naive-unsure 0.638 / 35%; Naive no-detail 0.497 / 47%. CC-Baseline over-diagnosis 7% (naive) to 51% (naive-unsure) to 74% (no detail), turn-budget exhaustion 49% on no-detail. SADE false-alarm rate stayed 20-34% regardless of wording. Cost per answered run: SADE $0.45, CC-B $0.43, ReAct $0.12; timeouts are 9% of runs but 23% of spend.
quote: the agents can test and refute a definite claim against the live network, while a vague report leaves nothing to refute
limits: Single judge model; ticket rewrites authored by the benchmark team. SADE and CC-B have different token budgets from ReAct, so over-diagnosis and cost are confounded with agent design.
agent_relevance: A verify gate should demand a checkable observation. When the report offers nothing to check, route to 'ask for or gather a checkable fact' instead of picking the nearest benign anomaly.

source: Tseng et al. (2026) SADE: Symptom-Aware Diagnostic Escalation for LLM-based network troubleshooting, arXiv 2605.04530
finding: A phase-gated policy based on the Cisco method (initial scan, four-layer deep scan, symptom-to-fault-family map, skill-driven localisation) beat ReAct on the NIKA benchmark and beat the same-backbone Claude Code baseline. The model-controlled comparison removes the objection that gains come from a better model.
numbers: 523 matched held-out NIKA cases, 11 unseen scenarios. RCA F1: SADE 0.77, Claude-Code baseline 0.55, ReAct (GPT-5) 0.44 (Fig. 1 states 0.40; the text of Section V says 0.44). Detection accuracy 0.85 vs 0.67 vs 0.68. Mean judge overall 4.32 vs 3.93 vs 3.80 (1-5 scale, gpt-5-mini). Gain over same backbone: +21.5 F1 points. Tool calls per session: SADE 19.9, ReAct 25.4, CC-B 26.7; per correct submission 27.2 vs 49.5 vs 51.5.
limits: Authors built the policy and the evaluation harness; judge is NIKA's gpt-5-mini protocol; one run per case is implied, no variance reported in the passages I read. Benchmark has fault injection that sometimes fails, which the authors patched with a rescue-and-verify pipeline. FaulT-Bench (d04) shows SADE over-diagnoses healthy networks most (24%); NOTE it is NOT independent: the first author and senior author are the same as SADE (checked on the arXiv author lists), and both use gpt-5-mini as judge.
agent_relevance: Best direct support for a phase-gated cycle over free ReAct with the model held fixed. Its lesson on healthy systems must be added: a negative-anomaly exit is only reachable after the deep scan, and FaulT-Bench says that is not enough.

source: Tseng et al. (2026) SADE token budget (Table VI, N = 523)
finding: The phase-gated agent used more input tokens than both baselines, so the win is not at equal tokens. Fewer tool calls does not mean fewer tokens.
numbers: Median input tokens: ReAct 55k, Claude-Code baseline 189k, SADE 344k (about 6.3x ReAct and 1.8x CC-B). Median output tokens 10k, 6k, 8k. SADE no-submission failures 3.6x fewer than same-backbone baseline.
limits: Token table is read from garbled extraction (columns checked against the stated min/Q1/median/Q3/max headers). No token-matched ablation is reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 remains open: no study matches tokens between a cycle and ReAct. Our own test must cap tokens per arm. The ratio to beat is roughly 1.8x tokens for +22 F1 points.

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) LLM-as-an-Investigator (SIA), arXiv 2606.13220: comparative table, judge and user study
finding: Evidence-first interactive diagnosis (competing hypotheses, targeted questions, weight updates, counterfactual critique, adjudication) scored highest on 100 forum-derived cases, but confidence intervals overlap with several baselines and the grader is an automatic LLM rubric.
numbers: 100 cases (36 electrical, 30 hydraulic, 34 mechanical) drawn from 303 threads. Final score /100 [95% CI]: SIA 79.2 [72.7, 83.7]; THK-int 72.8 [66.8, 79.8]; Ask-5 72.3 [64.7, 79.5]; ReAct 69.0 [60.5, 77.0]; BAS 67.3; THK 67.5; ToT 61.5 [52.5, 70.0]. Potential (oracle over candidates): SIA 89.2, initial potential 79.3, ToT 84.0. Hypotheses/questions: SIA 9.0 / 5.2; ReAct 12.7 / 2.8. Other backbones: SIA 75.4 vs 69.2 (GPT-5.6 Terra), 76.1 vs 68.4 (Claude Sonnet 5), margins +6.2 and +7.7 over THK-int. User study: 10 participants, Likert 1-5; SIA usefulness 4.6, clarity 4.7, trust 4.5, but perceived time efficiency 3.0 vs 4.8 for baseline.
limits: References are forum 'reported solutions', not verified ground truth. The user simulator and evaluator are LLMs. SIA-vs-ReAct CIs overlap (72.7-83.7 vs 60.5-77.0). SIA asks twice as many questions as ReAct, so it is not cost-matched. User study is 10 people on self-chosen problems.
agent_relevance: Independent-judge reproduction (gap 10) is not done: the evaluator is the authors' own rubric. Cross-backbone replication inside the paper is mild support. SIA's main novelty is keeping rivals alive until evidence separates them.

source: Marozzo and Lio (2026) SIA stress test with misleading user conjecture
finding: When the user adds a plausible but wrong cause to the problem, SIA kept most of its accuracy because it logs user conjectures as hypotheses, not facts.
numbers: 10 non-random cases, 20 paired inputs. Final score 80.0 control vs 76.0 challenged; potential 90.0 vs 85.0; exact diagnoses 6 vs 5; the wrong suggested cause was chosen in 2 of 10 challenged cases; score fell in 3.
limits: Tiny N, cases picked because they could support a plausible alternative; no significance test.
agent_relevance: Supports the rule 'user-stated causes enter S2 as candidates, not as S1 observations'. Evidence is weak (N=10).

source: Chen et al. (2025) AIOpsLab, arXiv 2501.06706: Noop (healthy system) detection problems and step limits
finding: Two detection problems had no fault injected. Only one agent (GPT-4 with shell) said the system was normal; the others reported false positives, mistaking ordinary workload for a fault.
numbers: Noop: 2 problems (one per microservice app). 1 of the tested agents correct. Step limit: ReAct and FLASH keep improving with more steps, FLASH peaks at 59.32% at 20 steps; GPT-3.5 gains nothing beyond 5 steps. Detection: only FLASH answered all detection problems correctly.
limits: N is 2 for the healthy-system test, so it is an anecdote, not a rate. Results are one run per agent.
agent_relevance: Second, independent signal that default LLM agents see faults in clean systems. Too small to size the effect; FaulT-Bench (d04) gives the size.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: intelligent information gathering with LLMs and Bayesian experimental design, ICLR 2026, arXiv 2508.21184
finding: Choosing each question by expected information gain computed in code over sampled hypotheses beat prompting the LLM to ask a good question. The ablation 'Implicit Maximization' gives the LLM the same candidate questions and lets it pick the most informative one; it did much worse than code-computed EIG. A deterministic equal-split rule ('Split', close to split-half) was a strong but lower baseline.
numbers: 20 Questions, 3 problem sets x 100 hidden entities, 6 LLMs. Average gain over Prompt-Only: +37.4 percentage points; success rate more than doubled in over half of setups and never decreased. Example row (GPT-4o, Animals, success %), column order inferred from the table header: Prompt-Only 45, Split 83, CoT 62, BED-LLM 93, Entropy 88, Data-Estimation 70, ICL-Beliefs 25, Implicit-Max 70. GPT-4o-mini Animals: 44, 78, 55, 88, 79, 64, 18, 47. SEM about 5 points per cell (n=100).
limits: Hidden item is a single entity in an open world, not a fault in a component graph. The answerer is an LLM. Table was extracted with columns separated; I matched columns to the header list and to the text ('Entropy slightly better than Split'), but exact cell labels are inferred. Cost is higher (many LLM calls per question).
agent_relevance: Gap 3 now has a direct LLM-vs-code comparison on a close task: code-computed selection over the same candidates beats LLM selection by a large margin. It still has not been run on realistic fault graphs, so keep gap 3 open for fault graphs but upgrade the claim for generic question choice.

source: Li et al. (2024) MediQ: question-asking LLMs and a benchmark for reliable interactive clinical reasoning, arXiv 2406.00922
finding: Simply prompting models to ask follow-up questions made diagnosis worse. Adding a confidence-based abstention step (decide whether to answer or ask) recovered and exceeded that, but a gap to full information remained.
numbers: iMEDQA (MedQA test, 1,273 cases) and iCRAFT-MD (140 dermatology cases); Llama-3, GPT-3.5, GPT-4. Question-asking without abstention: 11.3% accuracy drop versus answering from the same limited information. Abstention with rationale generation and self-consistency: +22.3% accuracy. Remaining gap to complete-information upper bound: 10.3%.
quote: prompting these models to ask questions results in an 11.3% accuracy drop
limits: Multiple-choice vignettes, simulated patient. Percent changes are as stated in the paper (relative vs absolute is not always clear in the abstract).
agent_relevance: Evidence for a signal-triggered rule (gap 6): ask or probe only when a confidence check says evidence is insufficient; always-on questioning hurt. The same 'answer or ask' gate is the natural place for a no-fault exit.

source: Li, Kim and Wang (2025) QuestBench: can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks? arXiv 2503.22674
finding: Even when a model can solve the fully specified problem, it often fails to pick the one question that would fill the missing fact.
numbers: Four task families solvable by asking at most one question (Logic-Q, Planning-Q, GSM-Q, GSME-Q). Models strong on GSM-Q and GSME-Q but only 40-50% accuracy on Logic-Q and Planning-Q.
limits: Multiple-choice choice among given questions; abstract-level numbers read here, per-model tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Choosing the next probe is a separate skill from solving; leaving it to the LLM alone is risky. Supports computing the probe from the candidate set in code.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey of self-correction, TACL, arXiv 2406.01297
finding: Across the literature, no work shows successful self-correction driven by feedback from a prompted LLM in fair settings, except in tasks where checking is much easier than generating (for example verifying each item of a list). Self-correction works when reliable external feedback exists (code interpreter, search, symbolic checker) and after large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Survey with no single pooled effect. Examples named as unfair: RCI prompting uses ground-truth answers; Reflexion uses exact match against the answer; Self-Refine uses weak initial prompts.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Secondary synthesis; written before late-2024 reasoning models. Its conclusion is about prompted self-feedback, not about every reflective structure.
agent_relevance: For gap 6: reflection should be triggered by an external signal (failed test, contradicted prediction, repeated action), and the verify gate in S4 should use a probe, not a self-critique. Always-on self-critique has no support.

source: Mamede et al. (2020) Immunising physicians against availability bias in diagnostic reasoning, BMJ Quality and Safety (PMC7362774), re-opened
finding: Correction to the earlier reading: the intervention was a knowledge-focused immunisation exercise (compare look-alike diagnoses with feedback, done a week before), not reflection in the moment. It helped only on vignettes that carried the bias.
numbers: N = 91 second-year internal medicine residents, 8 Brazilian hospitals. Accuracy (0-1) on bias-exposed vignettes: immunised 0.40 vs non-immunised 0.24, difference 0.16 (95% CI 0.05 to 0.27), p = 0.004. On non-bias vignettes: 0.36 vs 0.41, difference -0.05, p = 0.45. Interaction p = 0.02. Bias-inducing diagnosis given 0.30 vs 0.60 (p = 0.02). Target N was 98; enrolment was lower.
limits: Underpowered against its own plan; vignettes only. Effect shows on biased cases and not on neutral ones, a pattern a trigger-based design would exploit.
agent_relevance: K13 should say 'immunisation exercise with feedback', not 'forced reflection'. The pattern (no gain without a bias trigger) fits a signal-triggered rule.

source: Lambe, Hevey and Kelly (2018) Guided reflection interventions show no effect on diagnostic accuracy in medical students (PMC6265413), re-opened
finding: Guided reflection (listing two or six alternative diagnoses) did not improve final diagnoses of four fictional cases, and often changed correct answers into wrong ones. Counting a case as correct when the right answer was only among the alternatives made reflection look good (a scoring artefact).
numbers: 186 recruited; groups control 64, short 58, long 64 (accuracy table has smaller n and does not sum to 186). Strict accuracy: control 0.47 (SD 0.26), short 0.42, long 0.41; F(2,173)=0.841, p>0.05. Lenient (correct among alternatives): 0.47, 0.70, 0.72; F(2,175)=18.992, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.18. Changes of answer: short 16 corrected (38%) vs 26 backfired (62%); long 14 (50%) vs 14 (50%). Confidence change about 0.1 in both.
limits: Medical students, fictional cases, one session. Direction (strict score lower after reflection) is not significant.
agent_relevance: A warning for any scoring that credits 'considered the right cause': judge the final cause only. Always-on reflection can flip correct first answers.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation, arXiv 2505.06120
finding: When information arrives piece by piece, LLMs make early assumptions, jump to a final answer, then rely on that answer and do not recover. Most of the loss is unreliability, not lost ability.
numbers: 15 LLMs, 6 generation tasks, 200,000+ simulated conversations. Average drop from single-turn to multi-turn: 39% (abstract), with aptitude -15% and unreliability +112% (Fig. 1).
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover
limits: Generation tasks (code, SQL, math, summaries), not fault diagnosis. Closest evidence I opened for 'anchor on early answer' in LLMs.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 8: no study measures needless repairs after recall in LLMs, but early-commit-and-rely-on-it is documented. Supports forbidding a repair until a refuting probe has run.

source: Schmidgall et al. (2024) Addressing cognitive bias in medical language models (BiasMedQA), arXiv 2402.08113
finding: Planting a cognitive-bias cue in a clinical question lowers LLM accuracy by 10 to 26 percent depending on model. Warning the model about biases or showing a bias example helped GPT-4 but only modestly and not up to the no-bias level.
numbers: 1,273 USMLE questions, 7 biases, 6 LLMs. Unbiased accuracy: GPT-4 72.7%, Mixtral-8x7B 51.8%, GPT-3.5 49.7%, PMC-Llama-13B 33.4%. Mean drop by bias: false consensus 24.9%, frequency 18.2%, recency 12.9%, confirmation 8.1%. GPT-4 worst case -14.0% (false consensus), confirmation only -0.2%; GPT-3.5 average -37.4%. Bias education: GPT-4 frequency bias 0.627 to 0.720.
limits: Multiple-choice, injected bias text, not recall of a past fault. Authors admit the biases are crude.
agent_relevance: Shows LLMs follow planted cues; a past-case hint in the prompt may act like an availability cue. A reminder to test case-library retrieval for harm, not only benefit.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Automatic root cause analysis via large language models for cloud incidents (RCACopilot), EuroSys, arXiv 2305.15778
finding: The case-retrieval part here is retrieval of similar past incidents as few-shot reasoning examples. A year of Microsoft incidents shows why case libraries cover only part of the problem: many incidents repeat quickly, but a quarter are new.
numbers: Insight 2: 93.80% of recurring incidents reappear within 20 days. Insight 3: 163 of 653 incidents (24.96%) had a new root-cause category. Micro/Macro-F1: RCACopilot (GPT-4) 0.766/0.533, GPT-3.5 0.761/0.505, fine-tuned GPT 0.103/0.144, XGBoost 0.022/0.009, FastText 0.076/0.004, GPT-4 prompt without examples 0.026/0.004, GPT-4 embedding-only 0.257/0.122. Best few-shot setting: 5 examples, alpha 0.3; more examples did not always help. Diagnostic-collection module in use 4+ years across 30+ teams.
limits: Output is a company-specific category label, so the zero-shot 0.026 is mostly a label-format effect, not proof of case value. Judged by labels, not by human diagnosis quality. OCE satisfaction is reported only as 'most OCEs expressed satisfaction' with no counts.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: the only human signal is qualitative OCE feedback. Case libraries help most for recurring incidents and must fall back to first-principles search for the roughly one quarter of new ones.

source: Jacovi et al. (2023) A comprehensive evaluation of tool-assisted generation strategies, arXiv 2310.10062
finding: Fair comparison against strong no-tool baselines: tool-using prompting strategies (including ReAct-like and self-ask styles) were often not better, and cost far more tokens.
numbers: Abstract: strong no-tool baselines competitive across datasets, difficulty levels and models; tool strategies cost orders of magnitude more tokens without significant gains. Error review of 50 tool-assisted errors: retrieval setting 60% wrong tool input, 10% wrong tool output, 30% wrong inference; calculation setting 80% wrong input, 20% wrong inference. Tool use happened in 70-80% (SelfAsk) and over 90% (others) of runs.
limits: QA and arithmetic, not diagnosis; few-shot prompting era models.
agent_relevance: Supports the token-matched design for gap 1: always give the no-scaffold arm the same token budget, since scaffold gains often vanish under a fair baseline.
